result.draftText: He ran from praise as a young man and lived alone in a cave for three years. Later a raging Goth came to his gate and shouted at him to get up. Gregory says Benedict “rose not up from his reading”, and the Goth ended up at his feet.
result.concerns: Both halves are recorded across his whole life, not in one deed. The quiet half is explicit: he loved the wilderness and "dwelt alone with himself". The confident half is calm command, shown again and again: he turned down the monks, stayed calm when they poisoned him, stayed seated before a king, and would not stand up for a raging Goth. Gregory never files him under one of his four tempers by name, so calling him confident is our reading of those scenes. Earlier research (research.json, figures[10]) read his "mind of an old man" as grave and leaned it toward serious. The Dialogues record no sadness in him, though, so the Deep Well does not fit. A bonus for the Oak page is the Scholastica story (ch. 33). He would not be talked into staying, and Gregory's verdict is "of right she did more which loved more". That illustrates the Oak's cost, "It can be hard for anyone to correct you", from the same source. He also fled praise, which is the Oak's trap. Housekeeping: his portrait already appears on the Shepherd gift card, so he would show up twice in the report. A few scholars doubt that Gregory wrote the Dialogues. Naming him also fixes the contradiction the owner saw: the kindredNote "No saint is on record" has to go, and Mary of Bethany can stay in the Martha story as the Oak side of the opposite pair.

verdict.who: St Benedict of Nursia (c. 480-547), Gregory the Great, Dialogues Book 2
verdict.quoteProblems:
I downloaded https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_02_dialogues_book2.htm again, converted it to plain text and checked every quotation by exact substring match. All 12 are there word for word, and every chapter reference is right (prologue; ch. 1, 3, 15, 31, 33). The translation is 'P.W.' 1608, edited by Gardner in 1911, so it is public domain. I also checked the Latin (la.wikisource, Dialogi (Gregorius Magnus)/Liber II). The wording is accurate, but some quotations prove less than the candidate claims:
1. "with a resolute mind only to serve God" (prologue). The word "resolute" is the translator's. The Latin only says "soli Deo placere desiderans", meaning "desiring to please God alone". Drop it as evidence for the confident half.
2. "seeing him sitting afar off, he durst not come near" (ch. 15). This records Totila's fear and Benedict's name for holiness, not Benedict's temper. Use Benedict's own act from the same sentence instead: "he reprehended him for his wicked deeds". That also matches the confident grace line: "free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice".
3. "long time he denied them, saying that their manners were divers from his" (ch. 3). The quotation stops just before "yet at length, overcome with their entreaty, he gave his consent". So he gave in, which slightly undercuts "hard to correct". Fine as evidence that he knew his own mind. Do not use it for firmness.
4. "he that sitting still did appease the fury of that cruel Goth" (ch. 31). Gregory's sentence goes on to say this shows "he had received power to work all that which he did". Gregory's point is God's power in a miracle, not temperament. Gregory frames the Galla and Totila scenes as holiness.
5. The candidate's concern says "The Dialogues record no sadness in him." The cited English says otherwise. Ch. 17 (Theoprobus) reads "for the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad". That is a 1608 mistranslation. The Latin "nec tamen, ut vir Dei consueverat, orando plangeret sed moerendo" means he usually wept while praying, and this time he wept from grief over the coming sack of his abbey. So the Latin records no habitual sadness. But anyone who follows the link will find "sad", so the claim should be reworded.
6. Minor: "sitting before the gate, reading upon a book" drops the Latin "solum" ("sitting alone"). It is weak evidence of temper either way.
verdict.reasons:
QUIET HALF: recorded, strongly, in more than one way. As a youth he fled "the praises of men". He lived "three years unknown to all men" in a cave. After the poisoning he went back to the "wilderness which so much he loved, and dwelt alone with himself". The Latin is "dilectae solitudinis": a solitude he loved, which states a preference, not just an event. Gregory then explains "dwelt with himself" at length. If Benedict had kept governing the unruly monks, "being wearied daily with correcting of their faults, he should have had the less care of himself" (verified; the Latin says he would have lost his "modum tranquillitatis"). That is almost exactly the quiet make-up: a crowded load wears such a mind down. Worth adding. Gregory's Latin uses the quiet make-up's own word, tranquil, for him twice: "mente tranquilla" (ch. 3) and "modum tranquillitatis". Counter-evidence: in later life he founded twelve abbeys and brought the people round Monte Cassino to the faith "by his continual preaching". So he did carry heavy work. Still, the love of solitude is stated outright, and a fair reader would agree he was quiet.

CONFIDENT HALF: recorded as a pattern of behaviour, never named as a temper, so "partly". The scenes span his whole life, not one deed:
- Monks tried to poison him. He faced them "with a mild countenance and quiet mind" and forgave them.
- He rebuked King Totila for his crimes and told him his future "in few words".
- A raging Goth shouted "Rise up". The Goth ended at his feet, and Benedict still "rose not up from his reading".
- In a famine his monks lost heart. He "rebuked them modestly for their pusillanimity" (ch. 21, verified). That fits "You step up when others hang back".
- He would not be talked into staying the night with his sister: "by no persuasion would he agree unto that". Gregory's verdict, "of right she did more which loved more", fits the Oak's cost, "hard for anyone to correct you".
That matches the standard's own definition: steady, unshaken, commanding without anxiety, not needing approval. The weaknesses need saying. Gregory never files him under a temper by name. He presents the Totila and Galla scenes as God's power. And the "resolute mind" and Totila's-fear quotations do not prove what they are cited for.

COULD ANOTHER TEMPER FIT BETTER? I tested each:
- Serious (morose). For: his "mind of an old man" from youth. That line is the stock saint's-life "old head on young shoulders" and means maturity, not gloom. He also acts "in anger" twice, dismissing an unstable monk (ch. 25) and a disobedient cellarer (ch. 28). Against: the serious type's trap is a quarrel, "being right about how badly you have been treated". His record is the opposite. He forgave the poisoners. He "was far more sorry for" Florentius "than grieved for himself". He gave penance to a monk who rejoiced at Florentius' death. Serious fits worse.
- Careful. He withdrew once from Florentius, out of fear for his young monks, not for himself. Otherwise he was fearless before kings and Goths.
- Cheerful: no evidence.
So confident is the best reading, and the earlier research's lean to serious rested on the topos.

Would a fair reader agree? Yes, most readers know Benedict as calm, firm, authoritative and a lover of solitude. One real risk: Gregory's word for this temper is "the proud", and Benedict is the great teacher of humility (Rule, ch. 7). The card handles that by showing him running from praise, which is this temper's trap. It meets the owner's rule: "one half strongly and the other clearly is acceptable and must be said". It is richer evidence than several existing kindred; Isaiah rests on one sentence. I would not set `partial: true`, because it prints "partly like you" and both halves do match. I would call the fit "good" rather than "strong".

THE DRAFT CARD: it has no section numbers and no pronouns for God. The sentences are short enough, but there are two problems:
1. It reverses the source's order and drops the miracle. In Gregory, the prisoner's ropes fall off at Benedict's glance, and the Goth falls at his feet. Only then does Benedict still not rise. The draft's "rose not up..., and the Goth ended up at his feet" makes the calm itself seem to cause the Goth's surrender.
2. It shows the quiet half well but the confident half only once.
The fixed text below adds the poisoning scene and states the love of the wilderness.

HOUSEKEEPING: remove the kindredNote "No saint is on record with this temper". That line is the contradiction the owner saw. Keep the gregoryLine. Mary of Bethany can stay in the opposites story. Benedict's portrait is already on the Shepherd gift card (results.mjs line 624), so he may show up twice in one report. Some scholars doubt Gregory wrote the Dialogues; research.json already notes it. He is a man, as the owner hoped.
verdict.fixedText: As a young man he ran from praise and lived three years alone in a cave. Gregory says he loved the wilderness. He was hard to shake. When his own monks tried to poison him, he faced them “with a mild countenance and quiet mind”. When a raging Goth shouted at him to get up, the Goth ended at his feet instead. Gregory says Benedict still “rose not up from his reading”.

result.concerns: The confident half is strong and comes from Christ Himself. Gregory glosses the reed as a mind moved by "praise or detraction", which is exactly the Oak's trap, so John is the Oak who beat it. Chrysostom adds that John was not inconstant "by natural disposition", a statement about his nature. The quiet half is clear but weaker. He lived in the wilderness until his public life, he answered in few words, and he stepped aside for Christ. But his public life was preaching to crowds, including "brood of vipers" sermons, so a reader could file him as a Herald or a Forge. There is also a naming clash: tradition calls him the Forerunner and the herald of Christ, and our Herald type is a different type. verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched every source again. All nine quotations are word for word.

- Catena Aurea on Matthew 11, CCEL, Oxford translation of 1841 (public domain). All three Gregory lines match exactly, under "Greg., Hom in Ev. vi. 2". The Chrysostom lines come from the excerpt that follows "Chrys., Hom xxxvii", so "Homily 37" is correct.
- BSB, from biblehub. Matthew 11:7, Mark 6:18, Luke 1:80 (the footnote letter "g" after "spirit;" was dropped, as the candidate says), John 1:21 and John 3:30 all match exactly. The capital H in "He must increase" is the BSB's own.
- Picture. The Commons file is Geertgen tot Sint Jans, "John the Baptist in the Wilderness", dated "between circa 1480 and circa 1490", Gemäldegalerie Berlin 1631, public domain. The candidate has this right.

The wording is exact, but three items are used out of context or claim too much.

1. Chrysostom's "his abode in the desert" does not show a love of quiet. The full sentence is "for that he had not served the flesh is shewn by his raiment, his abode in the desert, his prison". It is evidence of self-denial. Jerome says the same in Letter 125 (NPNF, newadvent): John went to the desert to guard his chastity. The Fathers explain the desert as self-denial, not temperament. It cannot count toward the quiet half.
2. John 1:21 ("I am not." / "No.") is one exchange, and he keeps talking in 1:23 and 1:26-27. Luke 3:18 (BSB) says the opposite of "few words": "With these and many other exhortations, John proclaimed the good news to the people." Drop it as evidence of few words.
3. In the draft, "He grew up in the wilderness" goes past Luke 1:80. Luke says the child grew and "lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel". He does not say when John went there. Say "he lived in the wilderness".

Minor points:
- The Chrysostom fragment "But John was neither inconstant by natural disposition" breaks off mid-construction. It is verbatim but reads oddly if quoted to readers. Use it only internally.
- Mark 6:18 is a single rebuke, although "had been telling" shows it was repeated. By the standard it only supports the confident half; it cannot carry it. Mark 6:20 (BSB, verified on the same page) would add more: "Herod feared John and protected him".
verdict.reasons:
CONFIDENT HALF: recorded. It fairly meets the standard's "steadiness, being unshaken, not needing approval".
- Christ's own question in Matthew 11:7 denies that John was a reed.
- Gregory glosses the reed as a mind that bends "according as the breath of praise or detraction reaches it". He then says "no variety of circumstance bent him from his uprightness".
- Chrysostom speaks of his nature, not a single deed. He says John was not "inconstant by natural disposition" and had "an excellent nature".
- The Oak's grace line fits John closely. It turns the confidence into "the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice", and John before Herod is the classic example (Mark 6:18-20).

Two honest caveats:
- The Fathers praise this as a virtue ("uprightness", constancy of conviction). Chrysostom says Christ "clears John of fickleness" after the question John sent from prison. So the record is steadiness, not a temper prone to pride.
- The candidate's note calls John "the Oak who beat it". That is interpretation. Keep it off the card.

QUIET HALF: partly recorded.
- What is clearly on record: he lived in the wilderness before his ministry (Luke 1:80). He also refused attention (John 1:20, 1:27, 3:26-30). "He must increase; I must decrease" matches the Oak portrait's own line, "You do not need the room's attention".
- What is not on record: any love of stillness, or crowds wearing him down. The Fathers read the desert as self-denial (Chrysostom in the very passage cited; Jerome, Letter 125).
- His public life points the other way. People came from "all Judea" (Matthew 3:5). He preached "You brood of vipers" (Luke 3:7) and "many other exhortations" (Luke 3:18).

A fair reader would accept the sure half. They would push back on the quiet half unless the card admits that his preaching years were loud. By the standard this is one half strongly and the other clearly but thinly, so it is acceptable only if the card says so.

WHAT TO CHANGE:
- Mark the card partial.
- Say plainly on the card which half is weaker.
- Drop the Chrysostom desert line and John 1:21 as quiet evidence.
- Replace the kindredNote. The draft note says no saint is on record, which is exactly the contradiction the owner saw.
- Naming risk: tradition calls John the Forerunner, the herald of Christ. The quiz has a type called the Herald, and readers may object "surely a Herald". The admission of loud preaching years answers that ahead of time. Never use the word "herald" in his card.

STYLE:
- "Jesus asked ... wind”, and Gregory says ..." joins two sentences with a comma. Split it.
- A reader will not see that "a reed swaying in the wind" was a rhetorical no. Say what Jesus meant.
- Name "Gregory the Great" in full. The Still Water card names Gregory the Theologian, so plain "Gregory" is ambiguous.
- There are no section numbers in the draft, and the capital in "He must increase" is right.
- Dates "died c. AD 30" is an acceptable round figure. "man": true is correct.

verdict.who: St Menas, hermit of Samnium (Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 3, ch. 26)
verdict.quoteProblems:
None of the quotations is wrong. I fetched https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_03_dialogues_book3.htm again ("Gregory the Great, Dialogues (1911)"; the page says "All material on this page is in the public domain", transcribed by Roger Pearse, 2004). All seven quotations appear word for word in chapter 26, "of a solitary Monk called Menas", including the spellings "strook" and "aught". The problems are in how they are sorted, not in the wording.
(1) "he sat still, viewing them all in particular" is filed under the confident half. It is the opening of a clairvoyance wonder: he picks out Carterius's gift from the pile. It records neither confidence nor a temper.
(2) "He desired not to possess aught in this world, nor to seek for any thing" is filed under the quiet half. It is about poverty and possessions. It says nothing about quiet, few words or avoiding attention.
(3) "as his manner was, he would sharply have rebuked him" is what Carterius feared, not Gregory's own description. It still counts as a habit.
(4) Two quotations are miracle stories, not temper. After the rebuke the Lombard "fell down before him, and was tormented of a devil". The bears "so feared his stripes" is a wonder too.
(5) The candidate leaves out a line that cuts against the quiet half: "his manner was, by heavenly talk to inflame all such as of charity came to visit him". Visitors came regularly, neighbours sent gifts "every one upon certain days in the week" for him to give away, and "his name became famous". That describes a hermit who talked a lot, not a man of few words.
(6) Minor: the dates field paraphrase "lived 'some ten years since'" is fair to the English, but the clause is ambiguous. I did not check the Latin.
verdict.reasons:
A fair reader of chapter 26 would call Menas a fearless, wonder-working hermit who rebuked sin. They would not call him a self-assured man who loves quiet. Neither half meets the standard strongly, so "one half strongly, the other clearly" does not apply.

CONFIDENT: partly. What the chapter records as a habit is bold rebuke: "he would never spare them", "as his manner was, he would sharply have rebuked him". It records nothing about self-assurance, steadiness under strain, or not needing approval. Bold rebuke also does not tell the tempers apart. The site already uses exactly this evidence for the Forge (serious and restless): the Chrysostom card says "it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing". If rebuke is the proof of confidence here, it undercuts the Forge's evidence. The best defence is Gregory's own gloss in the Moralia, which the site already quotes for the confident temper once redeemed: "the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice". Menas fits that line. But Gregory never links Menas to the lifted-up temper, and linking them is our inference. The Lombard and the bears are miracles showing God's power through him. Reading a temper from them is the "single deed" guess the standard forbids.

QUIET: partly, at best. "led a solitary life" names a way of life, not a recorded love of quiet. Every hermit in the Dialogues would qualify on that line alone. The same paragraph says his habit was "heavenly talk" with a steady flow of visitors. He sent messages to sinners and rebuked them sharply. The Oak's own risk line is "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts": a quiet tongue. Menas's record is the opposite. He was a hermit who talked, not a quiet man.

OTHER. He is obscure, and easily confused with St Menas of Egypt. There is no picture of him. On the Oak card, a man who "drove off bears with a stick" and "would never spare" sinners reads as zeal, which is the Forge again, not as calm self-assurance. Using him would swap an honest "no one is on record" for a guess with a citation on it. That is worse for the owner, who wants a real match.

DRAFT CARD CHECK. The sentences are plain and short, with no section numbers and no pronouns of God to capitalise. One grammar error: "If he heard of a great sin ... 'he would never spare them'" leaves "them" with nothing to refer to. The card also shows no quiet half beyond "lived alone", and it presents a miracle (the bears) as if it showed his temper. If the lead overrules this rejection, use the corrected text in fixedText, marked partial.
verdict.fixedText: A hermit in Samnium who lived alone, with a few hives of bees as his only wealth. When a Lombard tried to take them, he rebuked the man to his face. Gregory says that if he heard someone had sinned gravely, “he would never spare them”. Yet he rebuked them “with true love to their souls”. He did not live in silence, though. Visitors came often, and he stirred them with talk of heaven. The record shows his boldness more clearly than his quiet.

verdict.reasons:
Reject. The quiet half is real. The confident half is not recorded. What is recorded is patience, and Gregory himself files patience as a virtue in a different pairing. It is holiness, which the standard excludes.

1. Quiet: yes, and clear. Dialogues: "secular men's company did he avoid: and his desire was always to pray and serve God". The Latin is even stronger ("vacare semper orationi concupiscens"). So is Homily 35: "tumultus devitabat hominum, crebris ac prolixioribus orationibus intentus erat" (he avoided the noise of crowds and gave himself to frequent, long prayers). This is typical praise for a monk, but it is stated as a lasting habit.

2. Confident: only steadiness, and both sources call it a grown virtue, not a temper.
- Dialogues: "to what great perfection he was arrived" (Latin "in quo virtutis culmine sedebat", the summit of virtue).
- Homily 35 tells the story as its "one example of keeping patience", in a sermon on Luke 21:19. It calls him "virtute patientiae singularis" and says "virtus patientiae in eo vehementer excreverat", the virtue of patience grew strongly in him.
- The Roman Martyrology sums him up as "a man of wonderful patience".
Nothing records self-assurance, stepping up, commanding, or being hard to correct. Nothing shows praise steering him.

3. Gregory's own map places him elsewhere. The Pastoral Rule, Part III (newadvent.org/fathers/36013.htm), treats "The forward and the fainthearted" (the confidence pair) apart from "The impatient and the patient". Stephen is Gregory's model of the patient. Gregory even sets patience against pride: "Better is the patient than the arrogant". The Oak's temper is Gregory's proud ("elati"), whose trap is praise. Filing Gregory's own model of patience under that temper would be read as a misreading of Gregory himself.

4. The Homily makes him the opposite of the Oak's costs. He counted anyone who harmed him a friend, gave thanks for insults ("reddebat contumeliis gratias"), and thought all his enemies helpers. A fair reader would call this meekness and humility. That matches Gregory's picture of the patient, not "Sure of yourself... It can be hard for anyone to correct you. Praise can steer you."

5. It clashes with the site's own precedent. On the Hearth, Antony's settled soul and cheerful face count as evidence of the cheerful temper. In the English the site prints, "pleasant countenance" invites the same reading here. That would put Stephen on the Hearth (cheerful and quiet), or nowhere, rather than on the Oak.

6. Only one scene is told. Gregory says his patience was lifelong, so the steadiness is a habit, not a single deed. But the habit is patience, not confidence.

Sum: the quiet half is clear. The confident half is recorded only as "hard to rattle", which the sources call holiness, and Gregory files it under the patient. It fails the rule "one half strongly and the other clearly". He is also an obscure local saint, easily confused with St Stephen the first martyr. The owner asked for a man who truly fits, and this one would not survive a discernment-minded reader.

I fetched all three sources again and checked every quotation. All 13 are word for word in the texts: Palladius, Lausiac History ch. 10 (Lowther Clarke, tertullian.org); Socrates IV.23 (Zenos, newadvent.org); and Budge, Paradise vol. 2 (archive.org djvu text). (1) The Theophilus saying is doubtful as a record of this Pambo. Theophilus was archbishop from 385 to 412. Palladius has Pambo die 'after a little while' once Melania arrived, which is the early 370s; the candidate itself says about 374, and the project's own research says c. 373. The saying is also set in Scete, but Palladius places Pambo on the mountain of Nitria. Keep it off the card and out of the evidence.
(2) Sayings 182 and 196 are in the part of Budge vol. 2 headed 'Questions and Answers on the Ascetic Rule', not the 'Counsels' where sayings 49, 376 and 621 sit. Both parts are covered by the volume's title, 'generally known as the Sayings of the Fathers', so the source label on the card is still fair. The internal citation should be exact.
(3) Page numbers are right to within a page.
(4) Copyright: Lowther Clarke (1918) is public domain in the US because it was published before 1929. It is not public domain in the UK (Clarke died in 1968). The project already quotes it in many research files, so this is a note, not a blocker. Budge (1907) and Zenos (1890) are public domain everywhere.
(5) Draft card: 'He went on weaving palm leaves' stretches the text a little. Palladius says he was 'sitting still and weaving palm-leaves' when he blessed her. Later he answered 'without even raising his head'. 'He sat weaving palm leaves and blessed her in one sentence' is exact.
verdict.reasons:
QUIET HALF: recorded, by three separate sources. Saying 196 names silence as one of his three virtues. Palladius has his disciples Origen and Ammonius say he never answered at once and often waited three months. Saying 376 says he 'doth not speak until God giveth him permission'. Socrates tells how he learned one psalm verse on guarding the tongue. One honest caveat: this is recorded as a discipline he worked at. Saying 196 lists silence with fasting and hand-work, and Socrates has him say he 'scarcely succeeded' after nineteen years. The project's own research.json already flagged 'Pambo slow to speak' as holiness won in adult life, not an inborn temper. The standard lists 'few words, not seeking attention', and Arsenius and Elijah qualified on the same kind of evidence, so this half passes.

CONFIDENT HALF: only partly recorded. The candidate's claim of 'several deeds' is overstated.
- Melania's scene: a patroness brings 300 pounds of silver. He keeps working, blesses her in one sentence, sends the money elsewhere and tells her to 'be silent' without looking up. This is real, first-hand evidence (she told Palladius) of self-possession, calm authority and not needing anyone's approval.
- Socrates' 'no need of counting': the same kind of story (gold handed over, a request to count it). Treat it as a second witness to one kind of scene, not a second deed.
- The Theophilus saying: its date and place do not fit (see quoteProblems). It is also mainly evidence of silence.
- 'Like a king who sitteth upon his throne': a stock picture of holy glory (Moses' shining face), shared in the same saying with Silvanus and Sisoes. That is holiness, not temper.
- 'I have not had to repent of any word': about guarding his speech, and in the same breath he says 'as one who has not even begun to be pious'.
- Palladius frames the Melania story as his suspicion of gold and silver (detachment), and Melania ends it with 'did the Lord manifest His power'.
So the confident half rests on one well-witnessed scene. The rule is never to infer a temper from a single deed, so this cannot be 'strong'. It is clearly more than a guess, though. The scene shows how he carried himself, not one brave act, and it matches the Oak's own portrait line exactly: 'You do not need the room's attention.'

COUNTER-EVIDENCE THE CANDIDATE LEFT OUT (checked; Budge saying 325): 'They used to say that the face of Abba Panbo never smiled or laughed.' That is a direct record of a grave face, which points toward the Serious temper, so a fair reader could file him with the Deep Well. Add to that Antony's 'Put no confidence in thine own righteousness', Socrates' story of him weeping over an actress, and Antony calling him a man who 'feared God so greatly'. Gregory's tempers are not exclusive, and the quiz already lets a reader lean two ways. But this is why 'partial', not 'strong'.

FAIR-READER JUDGMENT: a fair reader would agree he was unshakable, did not need approval and was sparing with words. They would not agree the sources record a 'lifted-up' temper. Include him with partial: true, which renders as 'partly like you'. Frame him as the Oak at its best: steady, unmoved by wealth or rank. Saying 49 fits the Oak's trap well: 'It is a much better thing for a man to hold his peace' (said about praising one's neighbour). He is a man, which the owner asked for.

REQUIRED CHANGES:
(a) The fit rating goes from 'strong' to partial.
(b) No Theophilus line and no 'king on his throne' line on the card or the page.
(c) The card must include his reason ('The One to Whom you brought them...'). The draft stops at 'without even raising his head', which reads as rude.
(d) The kindredNote now says 'No saint is on record with this temper', so it must be rewritten. Suggested: 'His quiet is well recorded. Only one story shows how steady he was, so we call him partly like you. Gregory does name this temper's risk. A quiet person can keep the tongue still while the mind grows proud.'
(e) Wrap the new quotations in Q() and save the Lausiac text where check-quotes.mjs reads its sources.
(f) Related to the owner's complaint: casting Mary of Bethany as the Oak in the Martha and Mary story rests only on the quiet half (she sat and listened). If Pambo becomes the Oak's kindred, the page stops contradicting itself. The Mary casting is still thin on the confident half, and it is worth a line to the owner.

verdict.reasons:
IS HE THE SAME MAN IN ALL THREE PLACES? Yes. Conferences 3.1, 10.2 and 18.15 all call him the priest of Scete and of Cassian's own community. Two of them give the same nickname. Isidore held the post before him (18.15). Cassian met him in person (3.2), so the source is close to him.

THE QUIET HALF IS RECORDED STRONGLY, AS A TRAIT OF CHARACTER. 18.15 says he "always delighted in dwelling in the desert as if with a sort of innate liking". That is the language of temper, not of one deed. 3.1 adds that he went deeper into the desert "with no human companions to disturb him". He hid in wilder places, so that the other hermits "only with great difficulty caught a glimpse of him". He kept one cell all his life. The small detail in 3.2 ("after a short silence") also fits. A fair reader would agree without hesitating.

THE CONFIDENT HALF IS ONLY PARTLY RECORDED. The attack on it:
(a) Cassian's own headline for him is humility and submission. 3.1 says he "was endowed with the virtue of submission" and that "by the practice of humility and obedience he mortified all his desires". 18.16 ends "let us imitate with all our might the humility of the latter". In the theft story he did not defend himself. He accepted a false charge and asked to do penance for about two weeks. That is the opposite of the Oak's "hard for anyone to correct you".
(b) "Not cast down in mind" and "could not be moved" are steadiness under trial, and Cassian says it came from trusting God ("fixed the hope of his heart... on Him"). That is close to the "holiness" the standard says does not count on its own.
(c) "Gravity" could point just as well to the Serious temper (the Deep Well) as to the Confident one.
(d) "Put him on a level with the Elders" is what other people thought of him, not his own self-assurance.
(e) The Easter letter is one episode, although it lasted a while: he argued with Serapion many times, then brought in Photinus and put him "in the midst" before all the brethren.
(f) The water bucket is one habit. It reads more as hard asceticism than as confidence.

What survives the attack: the brief's standard counts "steadiness, being unshaken, ... not needing approval". Cassian gives "gravity and steadfast constancy" as a trait seen "even in boyhood" and admired by great men. 18.16 speaks of "this steadfastness and constancy of the man". Nearly all the monks of Egypt were bitter about the bishop's letter, and the other three priests of Scete would not let it be read. He alone did, and he kept pressing the point in public. That is the Oak's "you step up when others hang back" and "hard to rattle". It is recorded plainly, though once.

So the fair reading is: quiet, strongly recorded. Sure of himself, clearly recorded as steadiness and independence of mind, not as boldness or pride. Cassian pairs it with humility. That meets "one half strongly and the other clearly", and the card must say it. It is not a guess, and the temper is not built on a single deed. It is weaker on the confident side than the Herald's kindred (Peter, the young Basil). He is a man, as the owner hoped.

THE DRAFT CARD: its quotations are accurate and its sentences are plain and short. It has no section numbers and no pronouns for God. The nickname is explained fairly (18.15 gives the reason). Two faults. (1) It never says the match is partial, which the standard requires. (2) Its only sign of the confident temper is "gravity and steadfast constancy", and "gravity" could suggest the Serious temper instead. The letter episode is the clearest evidence for the confident half, so add it in neutral words (leave the doctrine out, as the candidate advises), and add one line saying the match is partial. Keep the theft story off the card, because on its own it reads as meek. The corrected card is in fixedText. src stays "John Cassian, Conferences". Picture: none. result.draftText: A desert monk who kept a stone in his mouth for three years “until he had learned thoroughly how to hold his peace”. Monks came to test him because he was known for never letting his mind be disturbed. They insulted him to his face, and he calmly agreed with every charge but one.

result.concerns: Partial fit, and it should be marked partial. His steadiness is well recorded: the brothers had heard he never let his mind be disturbed, and they tested it. But his own reason for agreeing with the insults is humility ('The earlier things I accounted as profitable to my soul'), not self-assurance. The quiet half is a discipline he took on: the stone was there until he 'had learned' to hold his peace. That suggests silence did not come naturally, so it is not clearly his temper. Never quote the brothers' insults ('a whoremonger and a boastful man', 'a garrulous and talkative old man') as if they described him. They were a test, and he agreed with them out of humility. There is a strong detail for the Oak page, though. When his thoughts wanted to judge someone, he 'quieted his mind, and held his peace'. That is the cure for the very risk Gregory names for the Oak: a still tongue with a proud mind. He may serve better as that example on the Oak page than as a kindred card.

I fetched the source again: https://archive.org/download/paradiseorgarden02ann/paradiseorgarden02ann_djvu.txt (E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907; public domain in the US). All six quotations are there word for word, allowing for the OCR repairs the candidate already declared.
(1) The "ON one occasion certain brethren..." story is on p. 40, under the chapter heading "Of Patient Endurance". The stray margin "183." falls inside it, and removing it is correct. Budge's own bracket "[to any matter]" is kept.
(2) "I am not a heretic" matches, same story, p. 40.
(3) The Poemen line is saying 100 on p. 176. The OCR prints "Abbd"/"AbbaV" for Budge's "Abbâ". Writing it as plain "Abba" drops the circumflex, which is harmless.
(4) "Hold thy peace, old man..." is saying 500 on p. 253. Exact.
(5) The stone saying is saying 61. It starts on p. 15 and runs onto p. 16, with a page number and running head in between. Budge's own bracket "[and kept it there]" is kept. Exact.
(6) Saying 356 is on p. 80. "adfc" really is "act". Exact.
None of them comes from a copyrighted translation such as Ward's.

Problems are in the USE of the quotations, not their wording.
(a) Quotation 3 does not show confidence. "His mouth made him to be called Abba" means his words earned him the title while he was young. It records authority of speech, which if anything pulls against the quiet half.
(b) Quotation 4 is a single rebuke of another elder. The standard forbids reading a temper from one deed.
(c) In quotation 1 his steadiness is something he worked at ("took the greatest possible care"). His stated reason in the same story is humility: "The earlier things I accounted as profitable to my soul". It is not self-assurance.
(d) The candidate missed the best confident-sounding line. Saying 485, p. 252: "If it were Agathon, he would keep the command, and overcome the war." It reads as a teaching line in the third person, not a description of his nature.
(e) Budge's own introduction (vol. 1) reads the stone saying the way the candidate fears: "Agathon only learned to keep silent by holding a stone in his mouth for three years." So silence was a practice he had to learn, not his temper.

Draft card problems:
- "known for never letting his mind be disturbed" overstates the source, which says he "took the greatest possible care" that it should not be disturbed. That is effort, not a trait.
- "calmly" is not in the text.
- "agreed with every charge" leaves out WHY he agreed. A reader will think he admitted to being a "whoremonger", and will take humility for the Oak's self-assurance.

verdict.reasons:
A fair reader of Budge would not call Agathon sure-of-himself by nature, or quiet by nature. Both halves are recorded as ascetic disciplines he worked at, not as his temper.

The confident half. What the sources record is patient endurance. His reputation was that he "took the greatest possible care" to keep his mind undisturbed. When he was tested, he gave humility as his reason for accepting the insults. His own teaching is "The crown of the monk is humility" (p. 186 area, saying 315). The rest of his record is self-effacing charity: he gave away the knife, and spent four months nursing a sick stranger. This is holiness, the very kind the standard excludes. It is not Gregory's "elati" (the lifted-up, steered by praise).
- The Poemen line records authority of speech in a young man, not self-assurance.
- "Hold thy peace, old man" is one rebuke of one elder.
- The line "If it were Agathon, he would keep the command, and overcome the war" (saying 485) is the closest thing to a self-assured voice. It is still a teaching formula.

The quiet half. The stone was kept "until he had learned thoroughly how to hold his peace". Budge himself glosses it as "Agathon only learned to keep silent". That implies silence did not come naturally, which argues against a quiet temper. Poemen's "His mouth made him to be called Abba" says he was known for his speech. Nothing records a love of solitude or stillness beyond what every Scete monk had. Nothing matches Gregory's tranquil mind that gives way under a pile of business. He worked for months in a hired room in town.

So neither half is strong, and the standard needs at least one strong. Making him the Oak's kindred would be a guess dressed as a record. It would also swap the owner's "no saint" disappointment for a card that a discernment-minded reader could fairly pull apart.

Recommended use: not as a kindred card. Saying 356 is a real, exactly quoted remedy for the Oak's named risk ("For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts"). It could sit beside Gregory's risk line on the Oak page as "what helps". The fixed text below is written for that use. If the orchestrator still wants him as kindred, it must be marked partial. It must also say that he agreed to the insults out of humility, and that he learned silence rather than having it by nature.

verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched all 13 quotations again: the BSB chapters from bible.helloao.org, and Chrysostom's Homilies 10 and 37 on Matthew, Homilies 16 and 17 on John, and Jerome's Letter 125 from newadvent.org. Each one matches its source word for word. Two only looked different at first because New Advent's link markup adds stray spaces; the words are the same. All the translations are public domain (BSB, NPNF 1888-1893). The problems are in how some quotations are used:
(1) Mark 6:20 ("Herod feared John... a righteous and holy man") shows his holiness and Herod's fear. It says nothing about John's temper, so drop it from the confident half.
(2) John 3:30 ("He must increase; I must decrease") is humility and not needing attention. It belongs with the quiet half, not the confident one.
(3) Chrysostom's Homily 17 on John, "who regarded not the multitude...", is quoted without its context. The next sentence praises "the boldness of the loud-voiced herald", who spoke "not in a corner, not in the wilderness, but in the midst of the multitude". The same passage works against the quiet half, so do not use it on the Oak card without saying so.
(4) "steadfast and sure": in 1888 English "sure" means firm and reliable, not "self-assured". The echo of the Oak's "sure of yourself" comes from the translation. The phrase is also Chrysostom saying what Jesus meant, so "Chrysostom calls him" slightly overstates it. The stronger line in the same homily is Chrysostom's "But John, says He, neither was such a character by nature". It says outright that his firmness was his nature. I checked it and it is word for word.
(5) The draft says "When important men came to flatter him" as a fact. Scripture only says priests and Levites were sent to ask who he was (John 1:19). The flattery is Chrysostom's reading of their motive (Homily 16 on John). If it is used, the card must say it is Chrysostom's view.
(6) The context of the wilderness quotations: Jerome says John left home to protect his chastity, and Chrysostom (Homily 10) calls the wilderness a sign fitting for the forerunner. Both describe a calling and self-denial, not a temper that prefers quiet.
verdict.reasons:
THE CONFIDENT HALF IS RECORDED STRONGLY. This is more than holiness or one brave act. Jesus Himself describes John's character: "A reed swaying in the wind?" (Matthew 11:7). Chrysostom (Homily 37 on Matthew) says this means John was not fickle "by nature": he was "steadfast and sure", "one firmer than any rock", and he showed "firmness and fortitude". He could have won honour "merely by keeping silence" before Herod, and he did not. It is also a long pattern, not one crisis. He told crowds, soldiers and tax collectors what to do, rebuked the Pharisees, and rebuked Herod to his face. Gregory's temper here is the "lifted up" one, and John is famously humble. That is not a problem. The site's grace for this temper is pride bowed before God, turning into "the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice". John is the textbook case of that grace.
THE QUIET HALF IS RECORDED CLEARLY, BUT ONLY PARTLY. Solitude is on record as his way of life from childhood until he began to preach (Luke 1:80). Chrysostom says he was "holding intercourse with none among men, but with God alone continually". Jerome says he chose the desert over his parents' house. Not seeking attention is also recorded strongly: John 1:20, and John 3:26-30, where he was glad when everyone went to Jesus. That fits the Oak's line "You do not need the room's attention" almost exactly.
The case against: the Fathers explain the wilderness as his calling and his self-denial, not as a temper that loves quiet. His public work was loud. He calls himself "a voice of one calling" (John 1:23). Chrysostom calls him "the loud-voiced herald" and stresses that he spoke "in the midst of the multitude". The site's own figure quiz scores him "Says it" and "Confronts" (site/src/data/bible-figures.json). So he must never be described as soft-spoken or a man of few words. The honest claim is the long hidden life before his mission, a man nothing could move, and no need for applause. There is one point in his favour: even in his mission he stayed in the wilderness, and the crowds had to go out to him (Matthew 11:7).
Would a fair reader agree? Mostly, if the card leads with the wilderness years and his steadiness. Many readers will expect him under the Herald, because "herald" and "forerunner" are his traditional titles. Marking him as a partial match is the honest choice. This is still the same standard the site already used for Antony (the Hearth) and Arsenius (the Still Water), whose quiet half is also desert solitude.
CHECKING THE DRAFT CARD: No section marks. No pronouns for God that need capitals. The sentences are plain enough, but the second one joins two claims and should be split. The main faults are that it states the flattery as fact and that it leaves out Jesus' reed saying, which is the strongest evidence.

So the Oak's note "No saint is on record with this temper..." must be deleted or rewritten, or the contradiction the owner reported comes back in a new place. One possible replacement: "Once his time came, he preached boldly. What the sources stress is the long hidden life before it, and a man nothing could move." Once kindred exist, gregoryLine is no longer shown, so nothing needs to change there.
He is a man and a saint, which answers what the owner asked for. The picture checks out: Commons File:Geertgen_tot_Sint_Jans_004.jpg is public domain, 1192x1811, c.1480-90, and shows John sitting alone in the wilderness. It suits the Oak much better than the 564px Doré engraving, which shows him preaching to a crowd.

verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched every source again and checked each quote against it. All eight quotations are word for word: the McGiffert NPNF2 page at newadvent.org/fathers/250102.htm (1890, public domain) and BSB Acts 15:13, 15:19 and James 1:19 from bible.helloao.org. No quote has a wording problem, but four are used in ways the sources do not support.
(1) "entering alone into the temple" (II.23.6). The Greek on Perseus (Perseus:text:2008.01.0640, 2.23.6) reads: τούτῳ μόνῳ ἐξῆν εἰς τὰ ἅγια εἰσιέναι ... καὶ μόνος εἰσήρχετο εἰς τὸν ναόν. So "alone" carries on the claim just before it: only James was allowed into the holy place, and "naos" means the sanctuary itself. That is the legend of his special access, which the candidate's own notes say to leave out. It says nothing about wanting to be alone. The card's wording, "he went into the temple alone so often to pray", turns that legend into a love of solitude.
(2) "you are just, and do not respect persons" (II.23.10) is spoken by his enemies as flattery. It echoes Matthew 22:16 word for word, and McGiffert's page marks that link. It describes fairness, not self-assurance.
(3) Acts 15:13 is filed as quiet evidence ("he listens until the others are done"). In fact it is James taking the floor with "Brothers, listen to me!" That points toward the confident half. Waiting your turn in a council is ordinary procedure, not a temper.
(4) James 1:19 is advice to every reader, not a record of his own temper. Eusebius II.23.25, on the same page, says the letter's authorship "is disputed". The candidate admits this.
Also: the note on Acts 15:19 says he "decides". BSB Acts 15:22 has "the apostles and elders, with the whole church, decided", and the letter in 15:23 goes out from "The apostles and the elders". He gives his judgment. He does not rule alone.
verdict.reasons:
REJECT. The confident half is only partly recorded, and the quiet half is not recorded at all.

CONFIDENT HALF (partly). The standard rules out holiness and courage in a crisis. Most of the evidence is exactly that:
- "Greater boldness than they had anticipated" (II.23.2) is a martyr's confession under threat of death. That is one brave act in a crisis.
- "The Just" (II.23.4, 7) is a title for righteousness. II.23.2 says he earned it through "ascetic virtue and of piety".
- Praying for his killers (II.23.16) is holiness, and it copies Luke 23:34; McGiffert marks the link.
- The genuine signs of standing are Acts 15:19 ("It is my judgment"), Galatians 2:9 ("reputed to be pillars") and Acts 21:18-24, where James and the elders tell Paul "do what we advise you". These show his office and his authority. They do not describe a self-assured temper.
- The flattery scene is the best fit for the Oak's trap, but it is the weakest history. It is built to mirror Christ: the pinnacle (Matthew 4:5), the flatterers' words (Matthew 22:16), the Son of Man at the right hand coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64), and "forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Its dating is also wrong: "immediately Vespasian besieged them", though the siege came about five years later.
- Josephus is the earlier source (c. AD 93), and Eusebius quotes him in the same chapter (II.23.21-22). He records a trial before the Sanhedrin and a stoning. There is no pinnacle and no flattery.
- Even taken at face value, the scene shows a man praise could not move. It does not show a man who was lifted up or sure of himself. Gregory's elati are the proud, and nothing in these sources calls James proud. They show him on his knees begging forgiveness for the people.

QUIET HALF (not recorded). There are three pieces of evidence, and none holds:
- The "alone" in the temple is the special-access legend in the Greek (μόνος follows τούτῳ μόνῳ ἐξῆν), and the naos was hardly a place to be alone. A steady habit of prayer is devotion, not a temper. Restless saints prayed just as hard.
- Acts 15:13 is him calling for the floor.
- James 1:19 is teaching, from a letter whose authorship is disputed.
Every source shows a public leader instead. Acts 12:17 has "Send word to James". Acts 15 and 21 show him leading and directing. Hegesippus says many believed "on account of James" after he spoke to crowds.
One more verse points the other way. In John 7:3-5 (BSB), Jesus' brothers urge Him to "show Yourself to the world". That is said by all the brothers together before they believed, so it cannot be pinned on James either. It must not be used either way.

WOULD A FAIR READER AGREE? No. A fair reader of Eusebius II.23 meets an ascetic, a righteous man and a martyr. They do not meet a quiet person who is sure of himself. The pairing would be a guess built from holiness, one brave deed and a legend. The standard forbids exactly that.

THE DRAFT CARD. The sentences are plain and short. There are no section numbers. "Him" for Jesus is capitalised correctly. But the second sentence misstates the source ("alone" as solitude). The card never says it is only a partial match, which the standard requires. And nothing in it shows either half of the Oak to a reader; it reads as a holiness portrait.

Reject. The sources record holiness, not a confident temper.

1. The confident half is not recorded. In NPNF, "self-command" and "self-restraint... freed from the most tyrannical of passions" (4.7) mean that Joseph mastered his jealousy. Chrysostom's own words for him are "mildness", "mild and gentle", "obedience" and "a submissive mind". That is meekness, the opposite of Gregory's "elati", the lifted-up. "Not even at this did he shudder, but submits and obeys" (8.4) is about obedience in a crisis: Chrysostom's reason is "for the man was faithful". The standard excludes exactly that. "Unshaken" (5.2) is about faith resting on Isaiah (see the quote notes). Against all this, the same sources record fear or trouble six times: Matthew 2:22, Luke 2:48, and Homilies 4.10, 4.11 and 8.4 (twice). The Oak card says "It can be hard for anyone to correct you. 2. The quiet half is only partly recorded. It rests on one episode. "Resolved to divorce her quietly" (Matthew 1:19) means privately, to spare Mary. It is mercy and discretion in a single act, not a love of quiet. Chrysostom adds that he "did not even declare it to any one... but was thinking it over with himself" (4.10), which is the same episode. "Pondered" is one act of thinking something over. "One who studied the prophets" and "the subject of his meditations" (5.2) record that he was a thoughtful student of Scripture. "Scripture records not one word he said" is an argument from silence, and the card opens with it.

(1) Augustine, Sermon 53, gives his own reason for her silence in the very next sentence: "For if she were to be getting ready words to answer, she must remit her earnest attention to hear." So she kept quiet in order to keep listening. He does not say she was sure of herself.

(2) Sermon 54, "she sat in greater confidence", comes straight after Augustine imagines the opposite: "how, think we, did she fear, lest the Lord should say to her, Rise and help your sister?" Her confidence came after Christ took her side. It was not her nature.

(3) The Chrysostom quotation, Homily 62.3, stops in the middle of a sentence. The sentence finishes with her saying "Lord, if You had been here, my brother had not died". Martha said exactly the same words. The passage praises her faith and her "fervent" love. It also says both sisters believed "not in a right way", and in the same paragraph Chrysostom explains that Mary stayed at home because "the other had not yet been informed".

(4) Mark 14:6 does not name the woman. The words "why are you bothering her?" appear only in Mark. The card should use John 12:7 ("Leave her alone," Jesus replied). In any case, these are Jesus' words about her, not a record of her temper.

verdict.reasons:
REFUTED on the confident half. Nothing in the sources records a self-assured temper. That half is inferred from two silences, and the cited sources point the other way.

Augustine explains her silence as attention: if she stopped to find words, she would stop listening. He says she "committed her cause to the Judge", which is trust in Christ. He imagines her afraid until she was "excused". Chrysostom's passage is about her faith and love while she grieved. John 12 records no words from her at all. So "again she said nothing" builds a trait from a gap in the story. Mark 14 does not name her.

Now weigh this against what the Oak's confident half actually is. In results.mjs it is Gregory's "proud" (gregory: 'proud'). Its trap is praise, and its risk line is "his mind he exalts". Listing Mary as this type's saint tells readers the Fathers saw her as the lifted-up kind. They present her as the picture of humble listening: at His feet in Luke 10, falling at His feet in John 11:32, wiping His feet with her hair in John 12:3. A fair reader, and certainly a discernment-minded one, would object.

The quiet half is only partly recorded. Luke 10:39 records one scene. Augustine says she "in stillness heard His word". But Augustine and Gregory both say plainly that they are reading her as a FIGURE of a way of life, not describing her nature. Sermon 54 says: "in these two women the two lives are figured... the life of labour, and the life of quiet". Moralia VI.61 asks: "what is set forth by Mary... saving the life of contemplation?" John 11:20 ("Mary stayed at home") is not evidence of quiet. The house was full of mourners (11:19, 31). Chrysostom says she had not been told Jesus had come. When she heard, "she got up quickly" (11:29), fell at His feet and wept (11:32-33).

Even the quiet half does not single out the Oak. The same evidence fits the Still Water (careful and quiet) just as well.

The draft card also fails the page rules. Sentences 2 and 3 each stack three clauses. "Rushed about" is not in Luke, which says "distracted by all the preparations". "Again she said nothing" is an argument from silence. And the card repeats the Luke 10 story that the same report already prints in the opposite section. It has no section numbers and no pronouns for God, so no capitals were needed.

THE SITE CONTRADICTION the owner caught is real, and rejecting her as kindred does not fix it. The Martha and Mary opposite story holds for the busy and still half: Martha's "worried and upset" fits careful and restless well. It does not show Mary's temper. So the page should stop implying that she is an Oak by temper. Reword the kindredNote so it names her honestly (see fixedText). Also think about cutting "while Mary stayed at home" from the story, because Chrysostom explains that line as her not yet knowing. She is also not a man, which the owner hoped for, so no fit is lost by leaving her out.

verdict.fixedText: At court everyone flattered the emperor, and the bishops gave way. But “in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself.” No one ever saw him angry or excited: “he was always one and the same.” When crowds of visitors grew too much for him, he moved to a hidden cell outside the city.
verdict.reasons:
I tried to refute this and could not. Include him, framed as steadiness and authority, never pride.

Confident half (recorded, as steadiness and authority). A disciple who knew him describes it as a settled trait, not one deed. It shows in the Life:
- "always one and the same" (ch. 27)
- "the authority he unconsciously exerted" (ch. 25)
- "in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself" and "he commanded rather than entreated him" (ch. 20)

The same fearlessness comes back across many scenes. Before robbers he said he "never before had felt so safe" (ch. 5). He fought the Arians "almost single-handed" (ch. 6). He faced Valentinian (Dialogue II) and Maximus (Dialogue III, ch. 11-12), and at Trier the rival bishops "began to mutter and tremble" when he was coming. Those scenes fit the Oak's "You step up when others hang back. You are hard to rattle." They also fit Gregory's own grace line for this temper: pride bowed before God becomes "the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice".

What a skeptic can rightly say:
(a) Sulpicius stresses humility and meekness above all. Nothing records a proud nature, which is Gregory's "elati".
(b) His steadiness rests on trust in God. Twice an angel gives him courage: "go with confidence to the palace" (Dialogue II) and "resume your courage" (Dialogue III, ch. 13).
(c) He refused the diaconate, "crying out that he was unworthy", and had to be tricked into becoming bishop. The site files the same kind of reluctance under "careful" for Moses, Jeremiah and Gregory the Theologian.

Why these do not sink him. Gregory's four tempers are cheerful, gloomy, timid and proud. Martin is recorded as none of the other three. He is never seen "laughing", which rules out cheerful. He is never "enraged" or "lamenting", which rules out gloomy. He is openly fearless, which rules out timid. The reluctance in (c) is framed in the source as humility, not fear. So "confident" in its good form is the best of the four, and it has positive evidence behind it.

Quiet half (strongly recorded, as preference and habit):
- He "could not easily be drawn forth from his monastery" (ch. 9).
- He left the city because he could not "tolerate the disturbance caused by the numbers of those visiting it". He moved to a place so hidden that "he enjoyed in it the solitude of a hermit" (ch. 10).
- "his retired and tranquil life" (ch. 27).
- In church he sat alone before the service "as his custom was", while the other clergy exchanged courtesies (Dialogue II, ch. 1).

Caveat: he was also a busy, travelling bishop, and Sulpicius calls him "active" in conversation. The record does not show a man of few words. What it shows is someone who kept choosing quiet.

A fair reader of Sulpicius would accept: steady, commanding without anxiety, not needing the room, loving solitude. They would reject any hint of pride, so the card must not say "proud" or "sure of himself" about him.

The draft card is plain, short and has no section numbers. It needs no pronouns of God. One fix: the flattery belongs to everyone around the emperor, and the bishops "gave way" (fixed text above).

Gregory, whose book the test is built on, reads the reed as a mind bent by 'praise or detraction'. That is the Oak's own trap, which John withstood. 2. Gregory, whose scheme the test uses, reads the reed as a mind bent by "praise or detraction". Praise is exactly the confident temper's trap, and John stood against it.
3. This is a pattern, not one brave deed. John "had been telling" Herod, over and over (Mark 6:18; Matthew 14:4). He "openly declared" (John 1:20). One weak item: Mark 6:20 says Herod feared him "knowing that he was a righteous and holy man". That fear comes from his holiness, not his temper, so it should not carry weight.

QUIET HALF: CLEAR BUT NOT STRONG. The record shows a way of life and a lack of self-importance. No source says in words that he loved quiet, the way Abba Nastir says Elijah "loved silence". The evidence is still better than the candidate gives, and I verified these extra lines word for word:

- Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Matthew (newadvent 200110): he "dwelt entirely in the wilderness from his very swaddling clothes". Also: "neither did he keep them in the wilderness to take them about with him, but baptizing them ... he dismissed them". That fits "You do not need the room's attention".
- John 3:26-30: when told "everyone is going to Him", he answered "He must increase; I must decrease."
- John 1:35-37: he pointed his own two disciples to Jesus, and they left him to follow Jesus.
Against this, his public year was crowded and loud. Chrysostom's own Homily 10 even says "he went down unto the cities". So the concerns' line that he "stayed in the desert and let the crowds come" is slightly too tidy. Luke 3:3 also has him going "into all the region around the Jordan".
The test already has a precedent: Elijah, a fiery public prophet, sits under quiet (Deep Well) on the strength of his desert record. John comes "in the spirit and power of Elijah". On the site's own standard (one half strong, the other clear), he qualifies. I would not mark him partial: his quiet evidence is at least as good as Jeremiah's in the Still Water.

1. "Herald of the Word" is a traditional title for John, and he is the "voice of one calling in the wilderness". Some readers will ask why he is not the Herald. The answer is that heralding was his calling. His temper, as recorded, was firm and at home in the desert. The card should show the not-seeking-attention side so this reads naturally.
2. Tertullian (Against Marcion IV.18, verified) reads the prison question of Matthew 11:3 as John being "offended ... as a man". So an early Father does see wavering there. But Jesus's reed words are His answer to that question, and Chrysostom and Gregory both read them as clearing John. The card never mentions the question.

verdict.reasons:
I tried to refute this, and it partly holds.

WHY THE SOURCE COUNTS. It is the only early Life of Benedict. Gregory says he got it "by the relation of four of his disciples" and names them: Constantinus, Valentinianus, Simplicius and Honoratus. That counts as close to the man.

QUIET HALF: recorded, and strongly.
- Gregory calls it the "wilderness which so much he loved", where he "dwelt alone with himself".
- He "retired his cogitations within the closet of his own soul".
- He fled "the praises of men" after his first miracle.
- Governing monks went "contrary to his own mind".
- He "long time denied them" before he would take charge.
These are Gregory's own descriptions of what Benedict loved, not guesses.

CONFIDENT HALF: clear, but not strong.
For: calm and easy command show up across four separate scenes, so this is not one brave deed.
- The poisoning: "with a mild countenance and quiet mind", and "Did not I tell you before hand".
- Galla: he only lifted his eyes when a monk-killer shouted at him to rise.
- Riggo: "Put off, my good son", said in front of the whole court.
- Totila: he raised the prostrate king and rebuked him, "Much wickedness do you daily commit".
This matches the confident half as written: "hard to rattle", "commanding without anxiety", "not needing approval". It also matches Gregory's grace line for this temper, pride bowed before God turning into "the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice".

Against:
- Gregory never names Benedict's temper. Compare Antony's settled, cheerful face, or Gregory's own "sad and melancholy disposition".
- Every calm scene is also a miracle or a prophecy. A skeptic can call it the holy man's serenity, a stock feature of saints' Lives, rather than a temper.
- The same page records things that pull toward the SERIOUS temper, the Deep Well, where Gregory already sits:
  - "the mind of an old man" from youth;
  - ch. 17, "found him weeping very bitterly", and, in this English, "the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad". I did not fetch the Latin, and the 1608 wording may be garbled here.
  - two flashes of anger: ch. 25, "in anger bad him depart", and ch. 28, "Then in an anger he commanded others to take that glass with the oil";
  - "with great sorrow of mind" and "my weakness cannot bear" in ch. 32.
A fair reader could argue he belongs with the Deep Well.

Still, his calm under threat is the trait Gregory shows most often. Most of the serious signs are single moments with a clear cause. The exceptions are the "old man" line and the one "rather to be sad" clause.

VERDICT. The quiet half is strong and the confident half is clear, which meets the "one strongly, the other clearly" bar. So include him, but mark him partial (partial: true, which prints "partly like you"), not "strong". His evidence is no weaker than Isaiah's single "Here am I" for the Herald. He is a man, as the owner hoped.

verdict.reasons:
QUIET HALF: strong, and recorded by several independent sources. Palladius writes that he sat still weaving, blessed his visitor "in a sentence" and never answered at once. Socrates, Church History 4.23 (NPNF, Zenos 1890, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/26014.htm) says he learned only Psalm 39:1, "I said I will take heed to my ways, that I offend not with my tongue". Nineteen years later he said he had "scarcely succeeded". Budge's Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907, public domain, https://archive.org/details/paradiseorgarden02ann) adds three more. Book 2 ch. 1 no. 196: "We saw in Abba Pambo three virtues ... fasting ..., and silence, and abundant work of the hands." Book 2 ch. 1 no. 182: before the visiting archbishop he said, "If by my silence [we] are not helped, [we] shall not be builded by my word." Book 1 ch. 8 no. 376: "The custom of the old man is not to speak immediately, for he doth not speak until God giveth him permission to do so." Both archive.org scans give these lines the same way. Book 1 ch. 8 no. 376 also answers the worry that his slowness was the careful temper. The Sayings put it down to waiting on God, not to worry.

CONFIDENT HALF: present but thin, and holiness can explain most of it. The candidate's case rests on one episode (Melania). Palladius tells that episode to show that Pambo was "very suspicious of gold and silver", a virtue and not a temper. His other two supports fail. The deathbed line is humble, and the "as come from God" line credits his care. A fair reader would accept "hard to rattle" and "does not need the room's attention". The reason is that the evidence now shows it three separate times: the rich patron (Palladius), the archbishop (Sayings no. 182) and the demons, where he laughed "at your weakness ... because it needeth so many of you to carry a feather" (Book 1 ch. 8 no. 325). A fair reader would not find "sure of yourself" or "step up when others hang back" in any source. No source calls him bold, assured or lifted up. So "partly like you" is the honest label, and three independent episodes lift it above a single deed.

EVIDENCE AGAINST, which must be weighed and not hidden:
(a) Budge no. 325 says "the face of Abba Panbo never smiled or laughed". That is gravity, which could be read as the serious temper (the Deep Well). It is more likely ascetic discipline, but no card should call him easy or warm.
(b) He wept at an actress and blamed himself (Socrates). That is humility, not confidence.
(c) Antony told him, "Put no confidence in thine own righteousness" (Budge Book 2 ch. 1 no. 197). This is standard advice, and nothing should be read into it either way.
(d) The project's own research.json already warned that "Pambo slow to speak" records holiness won in adult life, not a native temper. The same is true of Antony and Arsenius, who are already kindred, so this is a site-wide standard and not a reason to reject him alone.
(e) Dates: Palladius has him dying soon after Melania's visit (c. 373), yet in chapter 46 he is exiled after it. Theophilus became archbishop only in 385. So the date of the archbishop story is uncertain. The card gives no timeline ("once", never "years later").

DRAFT CARD PROBLEMS, fixed above:
(1) "waited to be thanked" is wrong. He did bless her ("May God give you your reward"). She was waiting to be "honoured or glorified".
(2) The first sentence piles up commas. It is split into short sentences.
(3) "He never answered a question at once" is exactly the site's careful cost: "You wait to be sure, and the moment can pass". On the Oak card it points readers to the Still Water. It is replaced with the archbishop story, which shows both halves.
(4) The clipped deathbed boast is dropped.
There are no section numbers. The one pronoun for God ("Whom") is capitalised.

ALSO: once Pambo is added, the Oak's kindredNote ("No saint is on record with this temper") becomes false and must be rewritten. He is a man, as the owner hoped. No portrait of him is on the site yet. The Rijksmuseum print is CC0.
